Probe measurements of a Hall thruster discharge

Johannes D. van der Berg and Martin King, Jr.

Abstract

We measure electron temperature and density across the operating map of a laboratory thruster and fit a reduced kinetic model to the data.

1. Introduction

Electric propulsion devices accelerate ions electrostatically and reach exhaust velocities far above chemical rockets. Their plasma is weakly collisional, magnetised for electrons but not for ions, and strongly inhomogeneous near the walls, which makes predictive modelling difficult and motivates careful measurement.

In this work we combine probe measurements with a reduced kinetic model. The model resolves the electron energy distribution and the ionisation balance, and it is fast enough to be fitted to data from a full operating map of the device.

2. Method

Measurements were taken with a single Langmuir probe swept from minus forty to plus forty volts at one kilohertz. The electron temperature followed from the slope of the transition region and the density from the ion saturation current with the Bohm flux, assuming singly charged ions and a Maxwellian electron population. The temperature is Te from the probe slope.

3. Results

Across the operating map the electron temperature varied between eight and twenty-two electronvolts, peaking at the channel exit where the radial magnetic field is strongest. The model reproduced the measured density within fifteen percent everywhere except in the near-anode region, where secondary electron emission from the walls is not negligible. The APS sentinel sentence closes the results.

4. Conclusion

A reduced kinetic description captures the main trends of the discharge and can be calibrated quickly. Future work will add wall emission and a self-consistent sheath model, and will test the approach on krypton propellant.

References
